meaning: First admits what was just said, then adds that the reality is not as big as it sounds: “I say X, but actually ...”.
connection: Noun / plain form of verbs and adjectives + といっても

senses.label: Although I say ..., actually
senses.meaning: First admits a fact. Then points out that the real situation is smaller or less impressive than the listener might think. The tone is “don't imagine anything too grand”.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + といっても (「だ」 after nouns and な-adjectives is usually dropped)
examples: I can cook, but only simple things.
He's a company president, but it's a tiny company with only three employees.
It's a holiday, but just one day.

senses.label: At the start of a sentence
senses.meaning: Placed at the start of a sentence as a conjunction. It corrects or limits the previous sentence: “that said ...”, “well, ...”.
senses.connection: Previous sentence. + といっても、〜
examples: I'm going abroad next month. Well, just to Korea.
I recently started jogging. That said, only once a week.

senses.label: Casual 「といったって」
senses.meaning: 「といったって」 is a more casual spoken form. Same meaning, but stronger, often with a note of complaint or excuse.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + といったって
examples: Sure it's cheap, but it still costs 10,000 yen.

notes: The second half must scale the degree down (“it is not that impressive / not that big”). Adding something in the same direction or even more impressive does not work: ✕「社長といっても、大企業の社長だ」→ ○「社長といっても、社員三人の会社だ」.
It is mostly used about your own things, to sound modest. Using it to judge someone else's things (「お宅といっても狭いですね」, 「部長といっても…」) belittles them to their face and is very rude.
「〜と言ってもいい」 (“you could even say ...”) and 「何と言っても」 (“after all / above all”) look almost the same, but both affirm and emphasize, the opposite direction of this pattern. Do not misread them.
The sentence-initial use needs a complete sentence before it. The casual 「といったって」 sounds like an excuse or a complaint; with bosses or clients, use 「とはいえ」 or 「ただ、〜」 instead.

daily.title: When a friend praises you
daily.description: A friend says your Japanese is good, and you modestly add a qualification.
daily.example: I can speak Japanese, but only at the level of everyday conversation.

daily.title: Talking about vacation plans
daily.description: Explaining to a coworker that your “trip” is actually a short one.
daily.example: I call it a trip, but I'm just staying one night at a nearby hot spring.

daily.title: Talking about your house
daily.description: A friend thinks you have a big house, so you explain.
daily.example: We do have a yard, but it's really small.

work.title: Explaining a delay to a client
work.description: Reassuring the client that the delay will be short.
work.example: The delivery will be late, but only by two or three days.

work.title: Describing a former company
work.description: Talking about your previous job in an interview.
work.example: I was a manager, but I had only two people under me.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」, the te-form of 「言う」 (「言って」), and the concessive 「も」. Literally “even if you call it ...”, which came to mean “I say ..., but actually ...”.

similar.title: 〜とはいえ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both admit something first, then add a qualification or contrast. 「とはいえ」 is more written and formal, and its second half can be anything that goes against expectations. 「といっても」 is common in speech and focuses on “the actual degree is not that high”.

similar.title: 〜とはいうものの
similar.explanation: Same origin (both built on 「と言う」) and similar meaning: “although ..., ...”. 「とはいうものの」 leans written, and its second half is usually “it can't actually be done / falls short of expectations”. 「といっても」 is mostly used to correct the listener's impression of the degree.

similar.title: 〜といえども
similar.explanation: Same origin (「と言えども」): a formal, literary way of saying “even ..., still ...”. Typical uses are 「子供といえども」 and 「プロといえども」, stressing that no status is an exception. This is a different direction from 「といっても」's “it is actually not that ...”.

similar.title: 〜からといって
similar.explanation: Same origin (「から」 + 「と言って」). 「からといって」 denies a conclusion drawn from the first part (「高いからといって、いい物とは限らない」). 「といっても」 corrects an impression of degree and involves no reasoning.

formation: Built from the quoting particle 「と」 + 「言って」 (the te-form of 「言う」) + the concessive particle 「も」. 「Xと言って」 means “calling it X”; adding 「も」 turns it into “even if you call it X”. In other words, you first grant that the label fits, then 「も」 opens a concession, and what follows shows that the reality does not live up to the label. That is why the second half always scales the degree down. In the sentence-initial use, the whole previous sentence is what 「と」 quotes, and you then correct it.

meaning: Uses a topic as a trigger to say what it brings to mind: “speaking of ...”, “when it comes to ...”.
connection: Noun + といえば／と言えば

senses.label: Speaking of ... (association)
senses.meaning: Raises a topic, then names the typical thing it brings to mind first. Also used to pick up a topic someone else mentioned and bring up something related.
senses.connection: Noun + といえば (often followed by 「〜が有名だ」 or 「〜を思い出す」)
examples: When it comes to Kyoto, it has to be the temples.
Speaking of summer, it reminds me of fireworks festivals.
Speaking of hot springs, I went to Hakone last week.

senses.label: It is ..., I suppose
senses.meaning: 「AといえばAだが」 repeats the same word. You reluctantly admit it, then add a reservation. The tone is vague and not fully agreeing.
senses.connection: Adjective / noun + といえば + same word + だが／だけど
examples: It's convenient, I suppose, but it's way too expensive.
I guess I'm busy, but not so busy that I can't take a break.

senses.label: If I had to choose
senses.meaning: 「どちらかといえば」 means “if I had to pick one” or “relatively speaking”. Used to state a preference softly.
senses.connection: どちらか／どっちか + といえば
examples: If I had to choose, I prefer fish to meat.

notes: You cannot use 「といえば」 to check what the other person means: ✕「来週の会議といえば、月曜日のですか」→ ○「来週の会議というと、月曜日のですか」.
「AといえばAだが／けど」 is a reluctant admission with reservations. Saying 「おいしいといえばおいしいけど…」 about a gift or a dish someone made means “it's not that good” and is rude.
「〜と言えばいい」 (“you just need to say ...”) looks the same but means something completely different: 「ごめんと言えばいいのに」 = “you should have just said sorry”.
To express a preference or a criticism softly, Japanese speakers often say 「どちらかといえば〜」 (「どちらかといえば苦手です」). Saying 「嫌いです」 directly sounds blunt.

daily.title: Talking about travel with a friend
daily.description: A friend says they're going to Hokkaido, and you share what comes to mind.
daily.example: When it comes to Hokkaido, it's got to be crab.

daily.title: Picking up a topic
daily.description: A friend mentions movies, and you bring up something related.
daily.example: Speaking of movies, have you seen that new one yet?

daily.title: Answering about preferences
daily.description: Asked which you like, you answer softly.
daily.example: If I had to choose, I'd say I like winter more than summer.

work.title: Introducing a local specialty
work.description: Telling a visiting client about a local product.
work.example: This town is best known for its sake.

work.title: Shifting to a related topic in a meeting
work.description: Hearing one topic, you raise a related matter.
work.example: Speaking of the budget, has next year's plan been decided yet?

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 and 「言えば」, the conditional (ば) form of 「言う」. Literally “if you say ...”, which came to mean raising a topic and what it brings to mind.

similar.title: 〜というと
similar.explanation: Same origin (「と言う」 + 「と」). For association, the two are mostly interchangeable. But only 「というと」 can be used to check “by ..., do you mean ...?”. 「といえば」 is mostly used when you pick up a topic yourself and say what it reminds you of.

similar.title: 〜といったら (bringing up a topic)
similar.explanation: Same origin (「と言ったら」). It can also raise a topic and bring up an association, but it often adds exclamation or emphasis (「その寒さといったら…」 “oh, that cold ...”). 「といえば」 is a calm association.

similar.title: 〜ったら
similar.explanation: Same origin: a casual contraction of 「と言ったら」. 「母ったら」 brings up a person while showing annoyance or affection; it is no longer simple topic association.

similar.title: 〜ときたら
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both bring up a topic first. 「ときたら」 is almost always followed by a negative judgment or complaint (「うちの息子ときたら」). 「といえば」 is a neutral association.

formation: Built from the quoting particle 「と」 + 「言え」 (the conditional stem of 「言う」) + the conditional particle 「ば」. Literally, “if we talk about X”. The conditional sets X up as a topic, and the second half naturally becomes “what comes to mind from it”, hence the association meaning “speaking of X ...”. 「AといえばAだが」 means “if you insist on calling it A, then it is A”, which gives a reluctant admission and leads into a contrast. 「どちらかといえば」 means “if I had to say which side”, a soft way to show a preference.

meaning: Raises a topic and says what it brings to mind; also used to check what the other person means: “speaking of ...”, “you mean ...?”.
connection: Noun + というと／と言うと; plain form + というと

senses.label: When you mention ..., I think of
senses.meaning: Uses a topic as a cue and names what naturally comes to mind. Basically the same as 「といえば」.
senses.connection: Noun + というと (often followed by 「〜を思い浮かべる」 or 「〜のイメージがある」)
examples: When people hear “Japanese food”, many think of sushi.
Okinawa brings to mind an image of a blue sea.

senses.label: You mean ...?
senses.meaning: Repeats what the other person said to check what exactly they mean, or to ask them to explain. A polite tone. On its own, 「というと？」 means “What do you mean?”.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + というと、〜ですか; 「というと？」 at the start of a sentence
examples: By next week's meeting, do you mean the one on Monday?
A: This plan has a few problems. B: What do you mean?

senses.label: Polite 「といいますと」
senses.meaning: 「といいますと」 is the polite form. Common in business, to check what someone means or to develop a topic.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + といいますと
examples: When you say “this change”, which part do you mean?

notes: The checking question 「というと？」 is fine with friends, but with bosses or clients say 「と申しますと？」 or 「といいますと？」. Replying with just 「というと？」 sounds too casual.
「〜かというと、そうでもない」 (“if you ask whether ..., not really”) is a different pattern with a negative meaning. Reading it as the association 「というと」 flips the meaning completely.
In the association use, the second half is usually a common image (「〜を思い浮かべる人が多い」). If you just want to pick up the topic and talk about your own experience, 「といえば」 sounds more natural.

daily.title: Sharing impressions of a place
daily.description: A friend mentions a city, and you share your image of it.
daily.example: Osaka makes me think of takoyaki more than anything.

daily.title: Not following a friend
daily.description: A friend says something vague, and you ask them to be specific.
daily.example: You mean you're not going to see him anymore?

work.title: Checking in a meeting
work.description: Confirming with your boss which document they mean.
work.example: By that document, do you mean the one I sent you last week?

work.title: A client raises a concern
work.description: The client says there's a problem, and you ask for details.
work.example: When you say there's a problem, what points are you referring to?

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」, the verb 「言う」, and the conditional 「と」. Literally “when you say ...”, which led to two uses: association and checking.

similar.title: 〜といえば
similar.explanation: Same origin. For association, they are mostly interchangeable. To check what the other person said, use only 「というと」. To pick up a topic yourself and share a personal association, 「といえば」 is more common.

similar.title: 〜かというと
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「かというと」 follows a question and leads into a reason or an answer (「なぜかというと」), or forms 「〜かというと、そうでもない」 to deny something. 「というと」 follows a noun or a sentence and shows association or checking.

similar.title: 〜というのは
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「というのは」 defines something, explains a meaning, or gives a reason (“what ... means is ...”). 「というと」 is association or a checking question; it does not define.

similar.title: 〜といったら (bringing up a topic)
similar.explanation: Same origin and similar meaning: both raise a topic. 「といったら」 often adds exclamation and stresses degree (「その美しさといったら」). 「というと」 focuses on association and checking.

formation: Built from the quoting particle 「と」 + the verb 「言う」 + the conditional particle 「と」. Conditional 「と」 means “whenever ..., then naturally ...”, so 「Xというと」 is “as soon as X is mentioned, (one naturally) thinks of ...”, and the second half is usually an image most people share. In conversation it becomes “when you say X, (I take it) you mean ...?”, which gives the use of checking with the other person. The polite versions swap 「言う」 for 「いいます／申します」.

title: 〜ほど (degree)
meaning: Shows how great a degree is by giving a concrete example or comparison: “so ... that ...”, “to the point of ...”.
connection: Verb plain form / い-adjective / な-adjective + な + ほど

senses.label: So ... that (degree)
senses.meaning: Uses an exaggerated or concrete situation to show the degree of what follows: “so ... that ...”, “to the point of ...”. Often used with 「死ぬ」, 「泣きたい」, 「驚く」, etc.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective plain form + ほど + adjective / verb
examples: My feet hurt so much I wanted to cry.
I'm dead tired.
The ramen at this shop is surprisingly cheap.

senses.label: 「ほどだ」 at the end
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, it shows how far the earlier state went. 「〜ほどだった」 is used for the past.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective plain form + ほどだ／ほどです
examples: Yesterday it was so cold I didn't even want to go outside.
His Japanese is so good that people mistake him for a native speaker.

senses.label: 「ほどの」 + noun
senses.meaning: Modifies a noun: “a ... to the degree of ...”. Common forms are 「信じられないほどの」 and 「数えきれないほどの」.
senses.connection: Plain form + ほどの + noun; the noun 「山ほど」 = “a mountain of”, a huge amount
examples: An unbelievable number of people gathered.
I have a mountain of homework.

notes: In comparisons, 「ほど」 cannot mean “as ... as” in an affirmative sentence: ✕「兄は私ほど背が高い」→ ○「兄は私より背が高い」. 「AはBほど〜」 must be followed by a negative (“not as ... as”).
After a number or quantity, it means “about”: 「三日ほど休む」 = take about three days off, not degree. When you see 「ほど」, first check whether a quantity comes before it.
な-adjectives need 「な」, and nouns attach directly: ✕「きれいほど」→ ○「きれいなほど」. With nouns like 「山ほど」, and with 「死ぬほど」, there is no 「の」.
「死ぬほど」, 「殺したいほど」 and similar phrases are casual exaggerations. Saying 「死ぬほど忙しい」 to a boss or a client, or in formal writing, is inappropriate; use 「大変忙しい」 instead.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: Telling a friend how tiring overtime was.
daily.example: Yesterday I was so tired I could hardly stand.

daily.title: Recommending a place
daily.description: Recommending a shop to a friend with some exaggeration.
daily.example: The cake there is amazingly good.

daily.title: After a movie
daily.description: Talking with family about how funny a movie was.
daily.example: I laughed so hard I cried.

work.title: Reporting a busy event
work.description: Telling your boss how crowded a trade show was.
work.example: There were so many visitors that the venue couldn't hold them all.

work.title: A news report
work.description: The news describes how severe a disaster was.
work.example: It rained so hard that you couldn't see ahead.

etymology: 「ほど」 is written 「程」, originally meaning “degree, extent, limit”. After verbs and adjectives it means “to the degree of ...”. It shares its origin with 「ほど」 meaning “about” (amounts) and “not as ... as” (comparison).

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい (degree)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: for degree, they are mostly interchangeable. 「くらい」 is more casual. Only 「くらい」 can mean “the bare minimum / something trivial” (「それくらい自分でやれ」); for extreme exaggeration, 「ほど」 is more common.

similar.title: 〜ほど〜ない
similar.explanation: Same origin (both are 「程」). 「AはBほど〜ない」 is a comparison, “A is not as ... as B”, and must end in a negative. This pattern only describes a degree, with no comparison.

similar.title: 〜ば〜ほど
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜ば〜ほど」 means “the more ..., the more ...”: a change in the first part drives a change in the second. This pattern only describes one degree.

similar.title: 〜ほど〜はない
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「Aほど〜はない」 is a superlative, “nothing is more ... than A”. This pattern means “to the point of ...” and has no “most” meaning.

formation: 「ほど」 is the noun 「程」 (limit, degree), used here as a formal noun after a concrete situation (「泣きたい」, 「死ぬ」). 「泣きたいほど痛い」 means “it hurts to the point of ‘I want to cry’”: a concrete, often exaggerated scene is used as a measuring mark for the degree of the second half. Since 「ほど」 is a noun, it can take 「だ」 to become a predicate (「〜ほどだ」) or 「の」 to modify a noun (「〜ほどの人」).

meaning: Says that something is the highest in some respect; nothing is more ... than it: “nothing is as ... as ...”.
connection: Noun / verb dictionary form + ほど + adjective + noun + はない (いない)

senses.label: Nothing is more ... than
senses.meaning: Stresses that the first item is the most ... of all. It is the speaker's personal, high evaluation. Use 「〜はいない」 for people and 「〜はない」 for things and matters.
senses.connection: Noun + ほど + adjective + noun + はない／はいない
examples: There's no one kinder than her.
Nothing is more important than family.
There's no other mountain as beautiful as Mt. Fuji.

senses.label: Looking back on experience
senses.meaning: The past form 「〜はなかった」 looks back on experience: “there has never been anything so ...”. Often used with 「今年」, 「あの時」, 「今日」, etc.
senses.connection: Noun + ほど + adjective + noun + はなかった
examples: There's never been a summer as hot as this one.
I've never had a happier day in my life than today.

senses.label: The 「くらい」 form
senses.meaning: 「ほど」 can be replaced with 「くらい／ぐらい」 with the same meaning, but more casual. 「これほど〜ことはない」 is also very common.
senses.connection: Noun / verb dictionary form + くらい (ぐらい)／ほど + 〜ことはない
examples: Nothing is as lonely as eating alone.
Nothing could make me happier than this.

notes: Watch where 「は」 goes; getting it wrong reverses the meaning: 「彼女ほど優しい人はいない」 (she is the kindest) ↔ 「彼女はあの人ほど優しくない」 (she is not as kind as that person).
You need “adjective + noun” between 「ほど」 and 「はない」: ✕「富士山ほど美しいはない」→ ○「富士山ほど美しい山はない」.
Use 「いない」 for people and 「ない」 for things and matters: ✕「彼ほど頭のいい人はない」→ ○「彼ほど頭のいい人はいない」.

It is a very graceful way to praise someone. But with a negative word (「あの人ほど仕事ができない人はいない」), it becomes a harsh criticism, and saying it about a coworker, to their face or behind their back, is very rude.

daily.title: Praising a friend
daily.description: Introducing your close friend to someone.
daily.example: There's no friend more reliable than him.

daily.title: Complaining about summer
daily.description: Talking with family about this year's heat wave.
daily.example: There's never been a summer as hot as this one, has there?

daily.title: Relaxing in a hot spring
daily.description: What you say while soaking in a hot spring.
daily.example: Nothing feels as good as a hot spring after work.

work.title: A speech of thanks
work.description: Giving a speech at an award ceremony or farewell party.
work.example: Nothing makes me happier than having been able to work with all of you.

work.title: Stressing safety
work.description: Stressing “safety first” during training.
work.example: On site, nothing is more important than safety.

etymology: 「ほど」 (程) shows degree. 「Aほど〜はない」 literally means “a ... at the level of A does not exist”, so A is the most ... of all.

similar.title: 〜とは比べものにならない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean “far beyond”. 「とは比べものにならない」 directly compares two things and says the gap is huge. 「ほど〜はない」 puts A at the top without naming what it is compared to.

similar.title: 〜に限る
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can express “... is best”. 「に限る」 is the speaker's claim that doing something is the best choice (「夏はビールに限る」). 「ほど〜はない」 is a superlative judgment about the degree of something.

similar.title: 〜ほど〜ない
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「AはBほど〜ない」 is an ordinary comparison, “A is not as ... as B”. 「Aほど〜はない」 is “nothing is more ... than A”, a superlative.

similar.title: 〜ほど (degree)
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「ほど」 alone means “to the point of ...”, with no superlative. Only with 「〜はない」 does it become “nothing is more ... than”.

formation: Built from 「Aほど」 (“reaching the degree of A”) + “adjective + noun” + 「は」 (marking the focus of the negation) + 「ない／いない」. Literally, “a ... that reaches A's degree does not exist”. If nothing reaches A's degree, A is naturally the top, which gives the superlative “nothing is more ... than A”. 「は」 singles out “such a thing” and denies it, so the tone is strong.

meaning: Shows that a degree is excessive, beyond what is normal, often leading to a result: “too ... (so that ...)”.
connection: あまりに (も) + adjective / verb; あまりの + noun + に／で

senses.label: Too ...
senses.meaning: Used as an adverb before an adjective or verb to show that the degree is too high. Often followed by the result. 「あまりにも」 is stronger.
senses.connection: あまりに／あまりにも + adjective / verb
examples: It was too expensive, so I couldn't buy it.
This problem is just way too hard.
I was so tired that I fell asleep right away.

senses.label: Because of such extreme N
senses.meaning: 「あまりの + noun」 means “because ... was so extreme”. The noun usually expresses degree, such as 「暑さ」, 「痛み」, or 「ショック」. Often followed by 「に」 or 「で」.
senses.connection: あまりの + noun (〜さ／〜み, etc.) + に／で
examples: The heat was so intense that I almost collapsed.
The pain was so bad I couldn't even make a sound.
I was so shocked I couldn't say anything.

notes: Without 「に」, the meaning is the opposite: 「あまり高くない」 = not very expensive, 「あまりに高い」 = far too expensive. 「あまり」 is followed by a negative, 「あまりに」 by an affirmative.
「あまりの」 must be followed by a noun, so adjectives first become 「〜さ」: ✕「あまりの暑いに」→ ○「あまりの暑さに」.
The second half of 「あまりの〜に／で」 is a result that happens on its own; it cannot be an intention or a command: ✕「あまりの暑さに、窓を開けてください」.
「あまりにも〜」 is a strong judgment. Saying 「あまりにもひどい」 about someone's proposal or work is very hurtful; at work, say 「少し〜すぎるかと思います」 instead.

daily.title: Admiring scenery
daily.description: Seeing a breathtaking view on a trip.
daily.example: It was so beautiful I was lost for words.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Complaining to a friend about the summer heat.
daily.example: It's so hot I don't feel like doing anything.

daily.title: Hearing unexpected news
daily.description: Hearing that a friend is suddenly moving away.
daily.example: That's awfully sudden.

work.title: Commenting on a plan
work.description: Pointing out in a meeting that a plan is unrealistic.
work.example: I think this schedule is far too tight.

work.title: A news report
work.description: Reporting on the scene of an accident.
work.example: The impact was so strong that windows nearby shattered.

etymology: 「あまり」 is written 「余り」 and comes from the stem of the verb 「余る」 (“to be left over, to exceed”). “Going beyond the limit” came to mean “excessively, too”. 「に」 makes it an adverb.

similar.title: 〜あまり
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「余る」). 「Nのあまり／Vるあまり」 follows a noun or verb and means “because of too much ..., ...” (「心配のあまり」). This pattern is the adverb 「あまりに」 or 「あまりのN」.

similar.title: 〜あまりの〜に／〜あまりの〜で
similar.explanation: Same origin: a separate entry for the 「あまりの + noun + に／で」 form of this pattern, stressing “because ... was so extreme, a certain result happened”.

similar.title: 〜すぎる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express excess. 「すぎる」 attaches after a word (「高すぎる」), while 「あまりに」 is an adverb. They are often used together for emphasis: 「あまりにも高すぎる」.

similar.title: 〜あまり〜ない
similar.explanation: Same origin and the easiest to confuse. 「あまり〜ない」 takes a negative and means “not very ...”; 「あまりに」 takes an affirmative and means “too ...”.

formation: 「あまり」 is written 「余り」, the noun form of the verb 「余る」 (to exceed, to be left over), meaning “the part beyond the limit”. Adding the adverb-forming 「に」 gives “in a state beyond the limit”, i.e. “too ..., excessively”. Going beyond the limit tends to cause some consequence, so a result often follows (“couldn't afford it”, “collapsed”). 「あまりの + N」 is “an N beyond the limit”; adding the cause particle 「に／で」 gives “because it was so ..., ...”.

meaning: Says that, judging by what you'd expect from the first part, the result is surprising: “for ...”, “considering ...”, “although ... still ...”.
connection: Noun + の / verb and い-adjective plain form / な-adjective + な + わりに (割に)

senses.label: For ... (a standard)
senses.meaning: Measures against a standard given by a noun (age, price, etc.), and the result differs from what you'd expect. The surprise can be good or bad.
senses.connection: Noun + のわりに (は) (common with 「年齢」, 「値段」, 「見た目」)
examples: The food at this place is good for the price.
My father looks young for his age.

senses.label: Although ..., still
senses.meaning: After verbs and adjectives: judging by the first part, the second part is unexpected. Often implies “it doesn't match”. 「わりには」 is stronger.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective plain form / な-adjective + な + わりに (は)
examples: I studied a lot, but my score was still bad.
He eats a lot, but he doesn't gain weight.
This apartment is close to the station, yet it's quiet.

notes: It can easily offend when used about the other person. Saying 「お年のわりにお元気ですね」 to an older person reminds them they are old and is rude; just say 「いつもお元気ですね」.
Nouns need 「の」: ✕「値段わりに」→ ○「値段のわりに」. な-adjectives need 「な」: 「静かなわりに」.
When the first part is a specific status or a one-time fact, 「にしては」 is more common: 「初めてにしては上手だ」 sounds more natural than 「初めてのわりに」.
「わりに／わりと」 on its own before an adjective is an adverb meaning “fairly, quite” (「わりにおいしい」), not “out of proportion to ...”.

daily.title: Rating a restaurant
daily.description: Commenting after eating with a friend.
daily.example: This place is cheap, but the food's good.

daily.title: Talking about kids
daily.description: Mentioning how mature the neighbor's child is.
daily.example: That kid is small, but very responsible.

daily.title: Complaining about a movie
daily.description: After watching a much-hyped movie.
daily.example: For all the buzz, it was boring.

work.title: Analyzing results
work.description: Analyzing advertising results in a meeting.
work.example: We spent a lot on ads, but sales haven't gone up.

work.title: Evaluating a new hire
work.description: Commenting on a new employee to your boss.
work.example: He works fast for a newcomer.

etymology: 「わり」 is written 「割」, from the verb 「割る」, meaning “rate, proportion”. 「〜のわりに」 literally means “in proportion to ...”, which came to mean “compared to ... (it doesn't match)”.

similar.title: 〜にしては
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; often interchangeable. 「わりに」 mostly follows words with a scale such as age or price, and can follow adjectives directly. 「にしては」 mostly follows nouns or verbs for a status or a specific fact.

similar.title: 〜のに
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both show contrast or surprise. 「のに」 is a plain contrast, often with dissatisfaction. 「わりに」 stresses “out of proportion to the expected standard” and can be used for positive judgments.

similar.title: 〜くせに
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean “not matching ...”. 「くせに」 carries strong blame or contempt and is only negative. 「わりに」 is a more objective judgment, positive or negative.

formation: 「わり」 is written 「割」, from the verb 「割る」 (to divide), which came to mean “proportion, ratio”. 「Xのわりに」 is “in proportion to X”: you first estimate the “expected level” from X, then compare the second half with it. When the second half departs from that level, you get “out of proportion to X, unexpectedly”. Because it is about proportion, the first part is usually a word with a scale, such as age, price, or amount of study.

meaning: Judging by a role or condition in the first part, the second part is not what you'd expect: “for ...”, “considering it's ...”.
connection: Noun / verb plain form + にしては

senses.label: For ... (a role or condition)
senses.meaning: Uses the role or condition given by a noun as a standard, and the result is surprising. Usually an evaluation, good or bad.
senses.connection: Noun + にしては (common with 「初めて」, 「子供」, 「〜歳」)
examples: You did well for your first time.
That's a solid piece of writing for a ten-year-old.
For a cheap piece of clothing, this has good fabric.

senses.label: Given that ..., yet
senses.meaning: After a verb: “based on this fact, you'd expect ..., but actually ...”. Can also follow a fact you are guessing.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + にしては
examples: For someone who's lived in Japan ten years, his Japanese is poor.
For a joke, his face was awfully serious.

senses.label: Casual 「にしちゃ」
senses.meaning: 「にしちゃ」 is a casual contraction of 「にしては」. Used in relaxed talk among friends.
senses.connection: Noun / verb plain form + にしちゃ
examples: Pretty good for an amateur.

notes: The second half is the speaker's judgment; it cannot be an intention or a request: ✕「初めてにしては、頑張ってください」.
It implies “I didn't expect much”. Saying 「部長にしては上手ですね」 or 「新人にしてはいい」 to a superior or a senior suggests their level was low to begin with and is very rude.
To state your own position, use 「としては」: ✕「私にしては賛成です」→ ○「私としては賛成です」.
「〜にしてはいけない」 (“must not make it ...”) and 「〜にしてはどうですか」 (“how about making it ...?”) look the same but mean something completely different.

daily.title: Praising a friend's cooking
daily.description: A friend cooks for you for the first time.
daily.example: For your first try, this is really good!

daily.title: Commenting on the weather
daily.description: It's April, but cold.
daily.example: It's cold today for April, isn't it?

daily.title: Seeing a classmate's score
daily.description: A classmate who barely studied did well.
daily.example: That's a good score for someone who didn't study at all.

work.title: Reviewing a report
work.description: A boss comments on a new employee's report.
work.example: For someone in their first year, this report is well organized.

work.title: Analyzing data
work.description: Pointing out unusual numbers in a meeting.
work.example: Sales are far too low for this time of year.

etymology: Made of the particle 「に」, the te-form of 「する」 (「して」), and the contrastive 「は」. 「〜にする」 can mean “to take as ...”, so 「にしては」 is “if you take ... as the standard”.

similar.title: 〜わりに
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; often interchangeable. 「わりに」 can follow adjectives directly and usually goes with words of degree such as age or price. 「にしては」 mostly follows a status or a specific fact.

similar.title: 〜くせに
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both point out “not matching one's status”. 「くせに」 carries strong blame and contempt. 「にしては」 is a fairly neutral judgment and can also be praise.

similar.title: 〜にしても
similar.explanation: Same origin (both built from 「に」 + 「する」). 「にしても」 means “even if ...”: it admits something first and then gives an opinion. 「にしては」 means “by the standard of ..., the result is unexpectedly ...”.

formation: Built from the particle 「に」 + 「して」 (the te-form of 「する」) + the contrast particle 「は」. 「Xにする」 can mean “take as X, set as X”, so 「Xにしては」 is “if we measure by the standard of X”. Here 「は」 brings contrast: by the X standard, things should be one way, but they are not. So the second half is always a judgment that “doesn't match that status or condition”, positive or negative.

meaning: Criticizes or looks down on behavior that doesn't fit someone's status or a fact: “even though ...”, “despite being ...”.
connection: Noun + の / verb and い-adjective plain form / な-adjective + な + くせに

senses.label: Even though ... (critical)
senses.meaning: The first part is a person's status or a fact; the second is behavior that doesn't fit it. It carries strong annoyance, blame, or contempt. Both parts must have the same subject.
senses.connection: Noun + の / plain form (な-adjective + な) + くせに
examples: He knows, but he won't tell me.
You're just a kid. Don't be so cheeky.
He's bad at it, yet he's always bragging.

senses.label: Ending the sentence
senses.meaning: Placed at the end with the second part left out, to scold or tease. Common between close people, in a casual tone.
senses.connection: Plain form + くせに。
examples: Like you weren't late too.
You know you really like it.

senses.label: Casual 「くせして」
senses.meaning: 「くせして」 has the same meaning and is even more casual.
senses.connection: Noun + の / plain form + くせして
examples: You're a grown-up and you don't even know that?

notes: It carries contempt and blame. Never use it toward bosses, elders, or clients. Even with friends it sounds harsh and can start a fight.
The subject must be the same person in both halves: ✕「私が頼んだくせに、彼は来なかった」→ ○「私が頼んだのに、彼は来なかった」.
A sentence ending in just 「〜くせに。」 leaves out the blaming second half, and sounds even sharper than the full sentence. If you hear it, understand that the speaker is upset.
The 「くせ」 in 「癖になる」 (to get hooked, to become a habit) is the noun “habit”, not this pattern.

daily.title: A sibling fight
daily.description: An older sister scolds her brother for not helping.
daily.example: You've got nothing to do, and you still won't help at all!

daily.title: A friend playing dumb
daily.description: A friend pretends not to know, and you call them out.
daily.example: You know perfectly well. Stop playing dumb.

daily.title: Teasing a partner
daily.description: Your partner won't admit it, and you say with a smile:
daily.example: You missed me, and you know it.

work.title: In a novel
work.description: A character in a novel criticizes a coworker behind their back.
work.example: He's just a new guy, but he sure acts big.

etymology: 「くせ」 is written 「癖」, meaning “habit, bad trait”. 「〜くせに」 originally meant “with the nature of ..., yet ...”, and came to criticize behavior that doesn't fit.

similar.title: 〜のに
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean “even though ..., ...”. 「のに」 can be used for general surprise or regret, and the two halves can have different subjects. 「くせに」 needs the same subject and carries strong blame.

similar.title: 〜わりに
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both point out a mismatch. 「わりに」 is a fairly objective judgment and can be praise; 「くせに」 is only negative blame.

similar.title: 〜にしては
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「にしては」 judges by the standard of a status and can be positive or negative. 「くせに」 specifically blames someone because their words or actions don't match their status.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean “despite ..., still ...”. 「にもかかわらず」 is written and objective, with no contempt. 「くせに」 is spoken and strongly emotional.

formation: 「くせ」 is written 「癖」, originally “a (bad) habit, a flaw”. Here it is a formal noun followed by the contrastive 「に」. 「子供のくせに」 is roughly “having the nature and status of a child, and yet ...”, pointing out that someone's words or actions don't match who they are. Since 「癖」 is negative to begin with, this pattern naturally carries blame and contempt, so it is only used for negative judgments.

meaning: Admits or assumes the first part, then gives a contrary judgment or request: “even if ...”, “granted that ...”.
connection: Noun / plain form of verbs and adjectives + にしても

senses.label: Even if ..., still
senses.meaning: Admits the first part (or assumes it is true), but still gives the speaker's view, complaint, or request. The second part is usually an evaluation or criticism.
senses.connection: Plain form (nouns and な-adjectives attach directly) + にしても
examples: Even if you're busy, you should at least be able to get in touch.
Even as a joke, there are things you should and shouldn't say.
Even if you were going to be late, I wish you'd called.

senses.label: Whether A or B
senses.meaning: 「AにしてもBにしても」 lists two opposite or similar items: “in either case ...”.
senses.connection: Noun / verb + にしても + noun / verb + にしても
examples: Whether you agree or disagree, please give your reasons.
Whether it's meat or fish, I want to choose fresh ones.

senses.label: Even for ...; anyway
senses.meaning: 「Nにしても」 means “even from N's point of view”, raising a position. 「それにしても」 is a conjunction meaning “even so” or “anyway”.
senses.connection: Noun + にしても; それにしても、〜
examples: Even I can't accept this result.
Anyway, it sure is hot today.

notes: The second half is usually the speaker's judgment, criticism, or request (「〜はずだ」, 「〜べきだ」, 「〜てほしい」). For simply stating something that already happened, use 「のに」 or 「ても」.
It is often used to criticize someone gently (「遅れるにしても、連絡ぐらい…」). Said to a boss or a client, it sounds accusing; use 「ご連絡いただけると助かります」 instead.
「〜にしてもいい」 (“may make it ...”) and 「〜にしてもらう」 (“have someone make it ...”) look the same but mean something completely different: 「明日にしてもいいですか」 = “Can we move it to tomorrow?”.
In 「AにしてもBにしても」, A and B must be options of the same kind, and the second half is a judgment that applies to both.

daily.title: Scolding a late friend
daily.description: A friend is very late and didn't get in touch.
daily.example: Even if you're running late, at least let me know!

daily.title: Discussing a move with family
daily.description: Every option for where to live has drawbacks.
daily.example: Wherever we live, somewhere near a station would be nice.

daily.title: Small talk about the weather
daily.description: A casual remark when you meet.
daily.example: Anyway, it's been raining a lot lately, hasn't it?

work.title: Discussing proposals
work.description: Reminding everyone in a meeting to watch costs whichever plan they choose.
work.example: Whichever plan we choose, we need to review the costs.

work.title: Pointing out a problem
work.description: A boss comments on a subordinate's mistake.
work.example: Mistakes happen, but this report came far too late.

etymology: Made of the particle 「に」, the te-form of 「する」 (「して」), and the concessive 「も」. 「〜にする」 can mean “to take as ...”, so 「にしても」 is “even if you take it as ...”.

similar.title: 〜としても
similar.explanation: Same origin (both built from 「する」) and similar meaning. 「としても」 leans toward a pure hypothesis (“even supposing ...”). 「にしても」 usually admits a fact or something close to a fact, then gives an opinion about it.

similar.title: 〜にしろ・〜にせよ
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning as 「にしても」. 「にしろ／にせよ」 are more written and stiffer, mostly used in texts and formal settings.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「ても」 is the most ordinary concession. 「にしても」 usually carries the speaker's judgment or criticism.

similar.title: 〜としたところで／〜にしたところで
similar.explanation: Same origin and similar meaning. 「にしたところで」 means “even if it is ..., (it is no different)”, with a colder, more written tone. 「にしても」 has a wider range of uses.

formation: Built from the particle 「に」 + 「して」 (the te-form of 「する」) + the concessive particle 「も」. 「Xにする」 means “take as X, set as X”; adding 「も」 gives “even taking it as X (even admitting X)”. You first admit the first part, then 「も」 says “even so”, and you raise an opinion that doesn't fully agree with it, so the second half is usually a judgment or criticism. Paired as 「AにしてもBにしても」, it means “whether taken as A or as B”, i.e. “either way ...”.

meaning: Supposes the first part is true, but the second part is not affected: “even if ...”, “even supposing ...”.
connection: Noun + だ / plain form of verbs and adjectives + としても

senses.label: Even supposing ...
senses.meaning: Supposes a situation, yet the result or judgment stays the same. The first part is usually something that hasn't happened or is uncertain. Often paired with 「たとえ」 or 「仮に」.
senses.connection: Plain form (noun / な-adjective + だ) + としても
examples: Even if we hurry now, we probably won't make it.
Even if I fail, I won't regret it.
Even if that's true, I can't believe it.

senses.label: Also as ...
senses.meaning: 「Noun + としても」 is 「として」 (“as”) + 「も」: “from the standpoint of ... too”.
senses.connection: Noun + としても
examples: As a company, too, we can't ignore this problem.
He's famous both as a singer and as an actor.

senses.label: Casual 「としたって」
senses.meaning: 「としたって」 is the spoken form. Same meaning, more casual.
senses.connection: Plain form + としたって
examples: Even if I do go, it'll be next month.

notes: After a noun, you need 「だ」 for the hypothesis: 「先生だとしても」 = even if he is a teacher, 「先生としても」 = as a teacher, too. Without 「だ」 the meaning changes.
Replying 「それが本当だとしても」 to what someone told you hints “I don't really believe it”. Said to a boss or a client, it sounds like you doubt them and is very rude.
「何としても」 (“no matter what”) and 「〜ようとしても」 (“even if you try to ...”) are different structures, not this hypothetical concession.
For established facts, use 「ても」 or 「のに」; 「としても」 will be heard as hypothetical: ✕「昨日行ったとしても、会えなかった」 (if it actually happened) → ○「昨日行ったのに、会えなかった」.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: A friend is worried about failing an exam.
daily.example: Even if you fail, you can just take it again next year.

daily.title: Talking about a purchase
daily.description: Discussing with family whether to buy something expensive.
daily.example: Even if we buy it, let's wait for a sale.

work.title: Assessing risk
work.description: Explaining the impact of a worst-case scenario in a meeting.
work.example: Even if construction is delayed, the impact should be small.

work.title: A company statement
work.description: A spokesperson speaks at a press conference.
work.example: As a company, we too will do everything we can to prevent this from happening again.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」, the te-form of 「する」 (「して」), and the concessive 「も」. 「〜とする」 means “to suppose ...”, so 「としても」 is “even supposing ...”.

similar.title: 〜にしても
similar.explanation: Same origin (both built from 「する」) and similar meaning. 「にしても」 usually comments on a fact or something close to a fact. 「としても」 focuses on a pure hypothesis.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「ても」 works for both hypotheses and established facts. 「としても」 is only hypothetical, and the sense of “even if that were really the case” is clearer.

similar.title: たとえ〜ても
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; they are often used together: 「たとえ〜としても」. 「たとえ」 is an adverb that strengthens the hypothesis and does not show concession by itself.

similar.title: 〜としたところで／〜にしたところで
similar.explanation: Same origin (「と」 + 「する」) and similar meaning. 「としたところで」 stresses “even so, it is useless / no different”, with a rather negative tone. 「としても」 is just a neutral hypothetical concession.

formation: Built from the quoting particle 「と」 + 「して」 (the te-form of 「する」) + the concessive particle 「も」. 「Xとする」 means “set X as a premise, assume X”, so 「Xとしても」 is “even assuming X is true”. Because 「と」 quotes a full proposition, nouns and な-adjectives need 「だ」 first (「本当だとしても」). The core of the whole structure is “assumption”, so it stresses the hypothetical more than 「ても」 does.

meaning: The adverb 「たとえ」 strengthens a hypothesis: even under an extreme condition, the result won't change. “Even if ...”.
connection: たとえ + verb te-form / い-adjective くて + も; たとえ + noun / な-adjective + でも

senses.label: Even if ...
senses.meaning: Supposes an extreme or unfavorable condition and stresses that a decision or judgment won't change. 「たとえ」 makes the hypothesis stronger.
senses.connection: たとえ + verb te-form + も / い-adjective くても
examples: Even if it rains, the game will go ahead.
Even if my parents are against it, I want to keep this job.
Even if it's expensive, I want to buy something good.

senses.label: Even if it's N
senses.meaning: With a noun or な-adjective, use 「でも」: “even if it's ...”.
senses.connection: たとえ + noun / な-adjective + でも
examples: Even as a joke, you shouldn't say something like that.
Even children have to follow the rules.

senses.label: たとえ〜としても
senses.meaning: Combined with 「としても」 or 「たって」 for a clearer hypothesis. Common in both writing and speech.
senses.connection: たとえ + plain form + としても／たって
examples: Even if I end up alone, I'll see it through to the end.

notes: 「たとえ」 must pair with 「ても／でも／としても」, not with 「ば／たら」: ✕「たとえ雨が降れば」→ ○「たとえ雨が降っても」.
「たとえ」 is only for hypotheses. For facts that already happened, use 「のに」 or 「が」: ✕「たとえ雨が降ったが、試合は行われた」→ ○「雨が降ったが、試合は行われた」.
「例えば」 (for example) is a different word. If 「たとえ」 is not followed by 「ても」, do not read it as a concession.

daily.title: Stating your resolve
daily.description: Telling your family about your decision.
daily.example: Even if you're against it, I plan to study abroad.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend is worried they won't do well.
daily.example: Even if it doesn't go well, what matters is trying.

daily.title: In a novel
daily.description: A character in a novel makes a vow.
daily.example: Even if the whole world turns against you, I'll protect you.

work.title: Stressing the rules
work.description: Stressing the importance of rules during training.
work.example: Even for small amounts, always submit an expense claim.

work.title: Commitment to a project
work.description: A project leader states their position in a meeting.
work.example: Even if it takes time, we'll put quality first.

etymology: 「たとえ」 is generally thought to share its origin with the verb 「たとえる」 (“to compare, to liken”). It can be written 「仮令」 or 「縦令」, meaning “let's suppose”. With 「ても」, it became a fixed pair that stresses a hypothetical concession.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「ても」 alone can express concession; adding 「たとえ」 makes the hypothetical, emphatic tone stronger, often showing determination.

similar.title: 〜としても
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; often paired with 「たとえ」: 「たとえ〜としても」 stresses “even if that were really true” more than 「たとえ〜ても」.

similar.title: どんなに〜ても
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「どんなに〜ても」 stresses that no matter how high the degree, it is no use. 「たとえ〜ても」 stresses supposing a certain condition is true.

similar.title: 〜とも (concessive)
similar.explanation: The same meaning in a formal, literary form: 「たとえ〜とも」. Mostly seen in literature and formal writing.

formation: Made of the adverb 「たとえ」 working together with the concessive 「ても」 (te-form + 「も」). 「たとえ」 is generally thought to share its origin with 「たとえる」 (to compare, to use an analogy); its job is to announce “what follows is a supposed situation”, and it does not express concession by itself. What really means “it still doesn't change” is 「ても」. 「たとえ」 first points to an (often extreme) supposition, then 「ても」 says it doesn't affect the result, so the whole sentence stresses “the conclusion stays the same no matter what”, often expressing determination.

meaning: No matter how high the degree, the result doesn't change: “no matter how ...”, “however ...”.
connection: どんなに + verb te-form / い-adjective くて + も; どんなに + な-adjective / noun + でも

senses.label: No matter how ...
senses.meaning: Stresses that even if the first part is extreme, the second part is not affected. The second part is often negative, a regret, or a resolve.
senses.connection: どんなに + verb te-form + も / い-adjective くても
examples: No matter how hard I try, I can't beat him.
However busy I am, I eat breakfast.
No matter how much I practice, I don't get better.

senses.label: No matter how ... the N
senses.meaning: With a な-adjective or noun, use 「でも」.
senses.connection: どんなに + な-adjective / noun + でも
examples: No matter how hard it is, I'll keep going to the end.
No matter how famous a restaurant is, bad food is bad food.

senses.label: Casual and similar forms
senses.meaning: In speech, 「どんなに〜たって」 is used. 「どれだけ〜ても」 and 「どれほど〜ても」 mean the same.
senses.connection: どんなに + verb ta-form + って; どれだけ／どれほど + 〜ても
examples: No matter how much you hurry, you won't make it now.
No matter how much I explained, they didn't understand.

notes: Without 「ても」 it becomes an exclamation with a completely different meaning: 「どんなにうれしいか」 = how happy (I) would be!
「どんなに」 asks about degree, so it needs an adjective or verb that can be higher or lower. For a simple number of times, use 「何度〜ても」: ✕「どんなに行っても」→ ○「何度行っても」.
Saying 「どんなに頑張っても無理だ」 about someone's efforts rejects them completely and is very hurtful. Be careful using it with subordinates or coworkers.

daily.title: Cheering up a friend
daily.description: A friend is having a hard time at work.
daily.example: No matter how hard it gets, don't keep it all to yourself.

daily.title: Complaining about a diet
daily.description: Complaining to a friend that dieting isn't working.
daily.example: No matter how much I exercise, I don't lose any weight.

daily.title: A parent's warning
daily.description: A parent reminds their child to be careful.
daily.example: No matter how much of a hurry you're in, obey the traffic lights.

work.title: Stressing service principles
work.description: A store manager stresses customer service to staff.
work.example: No matter how busy it gets, please greet customers with a smile.

etymology: 「どんなに」 is the adverb form of 「どんな」 (“what kind of”) + 「に」, asking about degree. Combined with the concessive 「ても」, it forms the fixed pattern “no matter how ...”.

similar.title: いくら〜ても
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning; mostly interchangeable. 「いくら」 leans toward the number of times or amount of an action (「いくら言っても」); 「どんなに」 leans toward the degree of a state (「どんなに寒くても」).

similar.title: 〜ても (question word + ても)
similar.explanation: Both belong to the “question word + ても” family. 「何／誰／どこ + ても」 is a concession about “any target”; 「どんなに〜ても」 is specifically about degree.

similar.title: たとえ〜ても
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「たとえ」 stresses supposing a certain condition is true; 「どんなに」 stresses that even at the highest degree, the result is the same.

formation: 「どんな」 (what kind of) plus 「に」 becomes the adverb 「どんなに」, which asks “to what degree”. A question word combined with the concessive 「ても」 means “no matter ...” (like 「何をしても」). So 「どんなに〜ても」 is “no matter to what degree ...”, a concession covering every degree. Without 「ても」, 「どんなに〜か」 is still a question or exclamation, which shows that the concessive meaning comes from 「ても」.

meaning: No matter how many times an action is repeated or how high the degree, the result doesn't change: “no matter how much ...”.
connection: いくら + verb te-form / い-adjective くて + も; いくら + noun / な-adjective + でも

senses.label: No matter how much ...
senses.meaning: Stresses that even after repeating an action or reaching a high degree, the hoped-for result doesn't come. The second part is usually negative or a complaint.
senses.connection: いくら + verb te-form + も
examples: No matter how many times I tell them, the kids don't listen.
I waited and waited, but he never came.
No matter how hard I think, I can't figure out the answer.

senses.label: However ...
senses.meaning: With adjectives or nouns: “however ... it may be”. Also used to talk someone out of something: 「いくら〜でも〜すぎる」.
senses.connection: いくら + い-adjective くても / noun or な-adjective でも
examples: However cheap it is, I don't want this kind of thing.
Even if I love it, I can't eat it every day.

senses.label: 「いくら何でも」
senses.meaning: A set phrase meaning “no matter what, that's (going too far)”. Used to object to something excessive.
senses.connection: いくら何でも + 〜すぎる／ひどい, etc.
examples: Come on, that's way too harsh.

notes: 「いくら言えば分かるの？」 (“how many times do I have to tell you?”) is a scolding sentence, not a concession. Saying it to a boss or a client is extremely rude.
「いくらも〜ない」 = “not much”, 「いくらでも」 = “as much as you like”, and 「いくらですか」 = “how much is it?” are not this pattern.
「いくら何でも」 tells someone their words or actions are “going too far”. The tone is strong, so avoid it with bosses or clients.

etymology: 「いくら」 is written 「幾ら」. It was originally a question word asking about amount or degree (“how much”). With 「ても」 it means “no matter how much (or how many times) ...”.

similar.title: どんなに〜ても
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning. 「いくら」 usually stresses the number of times or amount of an action; 「どんなに」 usually stresses the degree of a state.

similar.title: 〜ても (question word + ても)
similar.explanation: Both belong to the “question word + ても” family. 「何回〜ても」 and 「誰が〜ても」 are concessions about number of times or about the person; 「いくら〜ても」 is one of the most common forms.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「ても」 only shows an ordinary concession; adding 「いくら」 stresses that “no matter how many times or how much”, the result doesn't change.

similar.title: 〜たって
similar.explanation: A casual spoken form with the same meaning, often paired with 「いくら」: 「いくら言ったって」. The tone is more relaxed.

formation: 「いくら」 is written 「幾ら」, a question word asking about quantity or degree (“how much”). A question word combined with the concessive 「ても」 means “no matter ...”, so 「いくら〜ても」 is “no matter how much (how many times, how far) ...”. Because its core is “how much”, it fits especially well with repeatable, cumulative actions such as 「言う」, 「待つ」 and 「考える」. 「いくら何でも」 is a fixed phrase meaning “no matter what you say, (that's too much)”.

meaning: The spoken form of 「ても」. Even if the first part is true, the second part is not affected: “even if ...”.
connection: Verb ta-form + って; い-adjective stem + く + たって; (godan verbs ending in ぐ・む・ぶ・ぬ) + だって

senses.label: Even if ...
senses.meaning: Same meaning as 「ても」, but very colloquial, with a casual and rather strong tone. Mostly used with friends and family.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + って (行ったって, 食べたって)
examples: Even if you run now, you won't make it.
There's no point worrying that much.
No matter how many times I tell him, he doesn't get it.

senses.label: Adjective 「くたって」
senses.meaning: With い-adjectives, use 「〜くたって」. 「なくたって」 means “even without / even if not ...”.
senses.connection: い-adjective minus い + くたって; 〜なくたって
examples: Even if it's expensive, I buy what I want.
You don't have to rush like that. It's fine.

senses.label: Sound change 「だって」
senses.meaning: For godan verbs ending in 「ぐ・む・ぶ・ぬ」, the ta-form uses 「だ」, so the form becomes 「だって」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form (〜んだ／〜いだ) + って → 〜んだって／〜いだって
examples: No matter how much I drink, I never get drunk.
It's no use hurrying now.

notes: It is very casual speech with an impatient tone. With bosses or clients, or in writing, use 「ても」 instead: ✕「部長、今から急いだって間に合いませんよ」.
It has the same form as the hearsay 「〜たって」 (= と言っていた): 「もう帰ったって」 = “I heard (he) already went home”, which is not a concession. Check whether another clause follows.
Connection: verbs ending in 「む・ぶ・ぬ・ぐ」 become 「〜んだって／〜いだって」, and adjectives use 「〜くたって」: ✕「飲んたって」「高いたって」→ ○「飲んだって」「高くたって」.

etymology: Generally thought to be a spoken variant of 「ても」, simplified from forms like 「〜たとて」 or 「〜たといって」 and combined with the past auxiliary 「た」 to form 「〜たって」.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「ても」 is the standard form and works in any situation; 「たって」 is spoken, with a more casual and stronger tone.

similar.title: 〜だって (even / also)
similar.explanation: A similar casual concession. 「Noun + だって」 means “even ...” (「子供だって」); 「たって」 follows verbs and adjectives.

similar.title: 〜たところで
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: also “even if ..., (it's no use)”. 「たところで」 stresses futility more and leans written; 「たって」 is an offhand concession.

similar.title: いくら〜ても
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; often combined with this pattern as 「いくら〜たって」 to stress “no matter how much ...”.

formation: Generally considered a spoken variant of 「ても」, simplified from forms like 「〜たとて」 and 「〜たといって」: the ta-form (past form) of a verb + 「って」. The ta-form shows “even if (that) is done”, and 「って」 carries the concession, so the whole thing equals 「〜ても」. Because it is built on the ta-form, it follows the same sound changes: 「飲む → 飲んだって」, 「急ぐ → 急いだって」 become 「だって」, and adjectives become 「高くたって」 (く + たって).
